instrument: Dubai RTA executive regulations for Law No. 9 of 2023 (autonomous vehicles)
edition_or_version: Gulf News article last updated 13 Dec 2025; Bracewell cites Administrative Resolution No. 939 of 2025
status_note: Adopted per press/law firm; official text not retrieved
requirement_paraphrase: Per Gulf News (13 Dec 2025), autonomous vehicles must meet seven technical and operational criteria for approval, including a manufacturer's certificate of successful road trials in its country of origin or another jurisdiction, evidence of conformity with relevant UAE or Gulf standards, and operational tests in Dubai demonstrating safety under local climatic conditions, with trial data shared with the RTA and identified issues addressed. Operators must notify the RTA of technical faults immediately and maintain integrated, secure electronic records of all operational data that may not be altered or deleted without prior RTA approval.
Three delivery robots run within about 3 km in a closely monitored environment; neither report names a permit, regulation or safety standard.

instrument: EASA AMC & GM to Reg (EU) 2019/947 (Annex to ED Decision 2025/018/R)
status_note: Document header reads 'Issue 1, Amendment 3'; EASA decision web page labels it 'Amendment 4' (conflict); later amendments after Oct 2026 not checked

instrument: EASA AMC & GM to Reg (EU) 2019/947 (Annex to ED Decision 2025/018/R)
status_note: Document header reads 'Issue 1, Amendment 3'; EASA decision web page labels it 'Amendment 4' (conflict); later amendments after Oct 2026 not checked
requirement_paraphrase: UAS components essential to safe operation must meet an airworthiness design standard. From SAIL IV EASA verification via a design verification report is expected; at SAIL V-VI a (restricted) type certificate under Part 21. EASA Special Condition Light-UAS is the recommended standard. Experimental flights may be accepted without recognised standards.

instrument: EASA AMC & GM to Reg (EU) 2019/947 (Annex to ED Decision 2025/018/R)
status_note: Document header reads 'Issue 1, Amendment 3'; EASA decision web page labels it 'Amendment 4' (conflict); later amendments after Oct 2026 not checked
requirement_paraphrase: UAS and external supporting systems must be designed to minimise hazards in a probable failure (SAIL III); strategy to detect, alert and manage malfunctions (SAIL IV); at SAIL V-VI failure-condition frequencies bounded, no single failure leading to catastrophic condition, and hazard-relevant software/AEH developed to an industry standard accepted by EASA.

instrument: EASA AMC & GM to Reg (EU) 2019/947 (Annex to ED Decision 2025/018/R)
status_note: Document header reads 'Issue 1, Amendment 3'; EASA decision web page labels it 'Amendment 4' (conflict); later amendments after Oct 2026 not checked
requirement_paraphrase: C3 link (C2 plus safety-relevant comms) performance, RF spectrum use and environmental effects must be adequate and stated in the flight manual; remote pilot must be able to monitor link performance continuously; licensed frequency bands for C2 required at the high integrity level (SAIL V-VI).

instrument: EASA AMC & GM to Reg (EU) 2019/947 (Annex to ED Decision 2025/018/R)
status_note: Document header reads 'Issue 1, Amendment 3'; EASA decision web page labels it 'Amendment 4' (conflict); later amendments after Oct 2026 not checked
clause_or_section_seen: OSO #08 (footnote on external systems) and OSO #13
requirement_paraphrase: Procedures must cover deterioration of external systems; EASA recommends identifying external systems (explicitly GNSS), their deterioration modes (complete GNSS loss, GDOP/PDOP, latency), means to detect them and procedures when detected (e.g. emergency recovery, manual control). OSO #13 lists GNSS navigation services among external services needing adequate performance, the interface with the provider possibly taking the form of an SLA or similar document.

instrument: EASA AMC & GM to Reg (EU) 2019/947 (Annex to ED Decision 2025/018/R)
status_note: Document header reads 'Issue 1, Amendment 3'; EASA decision web page labels it 'Amendment 4' (conflict); later amendments after Oct 2026 not checked
requirement_paraphrase: OSO #23: environmental conditions for safe operation defined in the flight manual, plus procedures and training to assess meteorological conditions before/during missions. OSO #24 (SAIL III and up): UAS designed to limit the effect of the defined environment; at SAIL IV-VI designed to environmental standards considered adequate (DO-160 given as example); rain example shows limits may be set to the representative envelope.

instrument: EASA AMC & GM to Reg (EU) 2019/947 (Annex to ED Decision 2025/018/R)
status_note: Document header reads 'Issue 1, Amendment 3'; EASA decision web page labels it 'Amendment 4' (conflict); later amendments after Oct 2026 not checked
requirement_paraphrase: Illustrative contingency-volume assumptions: GNSS accuracy 3 m, position holding error 3 m, map error 1 m, reaction time 1 s; reaction time may be shorter for fully automatic systems such as a geofence; GNSS altitude may be unreliable near large buildings.

Requires stand-alone GPS/SBAS equipment to meet RTCA DO-229E Section 2 (Class Gamma or Delta, DO-229E dated 15 Dec 2016) as modified by ETSO Appendices 2 and 4 (e.g. required Class Gamma path leg types; L1 C/A-code-only ranging and restricted data demodulation). New Section 1.8.3 on cybersecurity/GPS spoofing states it contains no new requirements; it recommends ('should') cross-checks and data-validity checks as guidance.
applies_to: Airborne GPS/SBAS equipment seeking ETSO marking

instrument: EASA Explanatory Note to ED Decision 2025/018/R
status_note: Page summary of the decision itself says Amendment 4; adoption date not stated on the page fetched
requirement_paraphrase: EASA replaced AMC1 Art. 11 with a European SORA 2.5; removed JARUS detailed cyber requirements but recommends a cybersecurity vulnerability assessment above SAIL III; SAIL IV requires an EASA design verification report and SAIL V-VI a Part 21 type certificate; PDRA AMC2-AMC6 not yet adapted; Member States may accept SORA 2.0 applications for a period (EASA recommends six months). Sec. 2.3 says Member States define the validity of existing SORA 2.0 authorisations; Sec. 3 (impact) anticipates two years.
